note: The Variations menu. Each variation has its rules in the engine (packages/chess-core/src/engine.js, chosen by the FEN prefix in `start`), a one-page rule sheet, a short lesson with Rooky and the animal friends as bots. `differs` marks a rule that is not like chess, in the sheet and in the lesson. Lesson and exercise lines are spoken from guide.json (`line`), recorded by tools/voice/record-guide.py. Variations with status `soon` are shown but cannot be played yet.

variants.name: Chaturanga
variants.tagline: The very first chess, from India
variants.blurb: The ancient Indian game that every kind of chess grew from. Its name means the four parts of an army: foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots. The pieces start where you know them, but the counsellor and the elephant move in the old, short way.

pieces.name: Raja
pieces.moves: One square in any direction, like the king today.

pieces.name: Mantri
pieces.moves: One square on a slant, and no further. He stands where the queen stands and grew into her.

pieces.name: Gaja
pieces.moves: Jumps exactly two squares on a slant, over anything in between. It stands where the bishop stands and grew into it.

pieces.name: Ashva
pieces.moves: Jumps in an L, just like the knight.

pieces.name: Ratha
pieces.moves: Slides along rows and columns, just like the rook.

pieces.name: Padati
pieces.moves: One square forward, even on the first move, and captures one square forward on a slant. On the far side he becomes a Mantri.

rules.title: The same start
rules.text: Every piece starts on the square of the piece it grew into: the Mantri on the queen's square, the Gaja on the bishops' squares.

rules.title: No castling
rules.text: The king walks to safety one step at a time.

rules.title: No en passant
rules.text: Soldiers never move two squares, so there is nothing to take in passing.

rules.title: Checkmate wins
rules.text: Trap the enemy king so it cannot escape, just like in chess.

rules.title: A bare king loses
rules.text: Capture every enemy piece except the king and you win. If they can capture your last piece straight back, it is a draw instead.

rules.title: No move at all loses
rules.text: If a player is not in check but has no legal move, the player who trapped them wins. In chess this is stalemate, a draw.

rules.title: Draws
rules.text: Repeating the same position, or fifty moves with no capture and no soldier move, can end the game as a draw, as in chess.

notes: Rules changed from place to place over the centuries. Chackmate plays one common version, close to shatranj, the Persian game that came from it.
Move lists write the Mantri as M and the Gaja as G. Saved games (PGN) use Q and B, the pieces they grew into.

lesson.title: Chess as it began
objectives: Move the Mantri and the Gaja
Win the old ways: bare king and no moves

hints: One small step, on a slant.
Exactly two squares on a slant.
The Gaja jumps over the pawn on c5, and can capture on b6.
Your chariot can reach Black's last piece.

exercises.explain: In chaturanga a soldier always becomes a Mantri, the counsellor.

hints: Black's pawn is stuck. Can the king move anywhere?
Use the chariot to guard the b-file.

variants.name: Chess960
variants.blurb: The pieces on the back row are shuffled before every game, so you have to think from the very first move.

rules.title: A shuffled back row
rules.text: Before each game the pieces on the back row are set out in one of 960 orders. Every game can start differently.

rules.title: A mirror image
rules.text: Black's pieces copy White's, file by file, so both armies start the same. The pawns stand where they always do.

rules.title: Two rules for the shuffle
rules.text: The two bishops always start on squares of different colours, and the king always stands somewhere between the two rooks.

rules.title: Castling
rules.text: The king lands on the g-file (king's side) or the c-file (queen's side), and the rook lands right next to it on the f-file or the d-file, wherever they started. To castle, move your king onto the rook.

rules.title: When you may castle
rules.text: As in chess: neither piece has moved, the squares they cross are empty, and the king is not in check, does not pass through check and does not land in check.

rules.title: Everything else
rules.text: Moves, captures, checkmate and draws are just like chess.

notes: Bobby Fischer, a world champion, invented Chess960 so that players would think at the board instead of remembering openings. Each start has a number from 0 to 959; number 518 is the usual chess start.

lesson.title: Shuffle the back row
objectives: Know how a Chess960 start is made
Castle when the king and rook start somewhere new

hints: Pick up your king and put it on the rook on h1.
The king goes to g1 and the rook to f1.
This time castle towards the a-file: put your king on the rook on a1.
The king goes to c1 and the rook to d1.

options: On the g-file, with the rook beside it on the f-file
exercises.explain: However the back row starts, castling ends just like in chess.

options: The king stands between the two rooks
The queen is always on d1
The knights always start next to the king
exercises.explain: That rule keeps castling possible on both sides.

variants.name: Xiangqi
variants.blurb: Chinese chess, played on the lines of the board with a river in the middle, cannons, and generals who never leave their palace.

variants.name: King of the Hill
variants.tagline: Race your king to the middle
variants.blurb: Win by checkmate, or by walking your king safely onto one of the four centre squares.

rules.title: The hill
rules.text: The four squares in the middle of the board, d4, e4, d5 and e5, are the hill. They glow on the board.

rules.title: Climb the hill to win
rules.text: Move your king onto any hill square and you win at once.

rules.title: Safely
rules.text: As always, a king may never step onto a square an enemy piece attacks, so a guarded hill square is closed to it.

rules.title: Checkmate wins too
rules.text: Trap the enemy king and you win, just like in chess.

rules.title: No dead draws
rules.text: Even a lone king can still walk to the hill, so a game is not drawn just because few pieces are left.

rules.title: Everything else
rules.text: The pieces, castling, en passant and the other draws are just like chess.

lesson.title: Race to the hill
objectives: Stop the other king getting there first

exercises.yes: You are on the hill. You win!
exercises.no: That square is not on the hill. Try again.
hints: The hill is the four squares in the middle.
Step up to d4 or e4.
Black's king wants d5 or e5.
Guard the whole fifth row with your rook.

exercises.yes: Only e4 was safe. You win!
exercises.no: That square is not on the hill. Try again.
hints: The bishop on b6 guards d4. Look for another hill square.
Your king can still step onto e4.

variants.name: Three-check
variants.blurb: Give check three times and you win, even before checkmate.

rules.title: Count your checks
rules.text: Every time you put the enemy king in check, your counter goes up by one. The counters sit beside the players' names.

rules.title: Three checks win
rules.text: Give your third check and you win at once, even if the king could escape.

rules.title: Checkmate wins too
rules.text: Trap the enemy king and you win, just like in chess.

rules.title: No dead draws
rules.text: While a side still has a piece that could give check, the game is not drawn for lack of pieces.

rules.title: Everything else
rules.text: The pieces, castling, en passant and the other draws are just like chess.

lesson.title: Three checks win
objectives: Keep your own king out of reach

exercises.no: That is not a check. Try again.
hints: You have given two checks already.
Any check wins now: try the rook.

exercises.no: That is not a check. Try again.
hints: Which white piece can reach the king?
The knight can jump to d6 or f6.

exercises.explain: The third check ends the game, even if the king could escape.
